Please read this carefully:

<document>
# Reduced Working Time at Full Pay: Results from a Six-Month Multi-Organisation Pilot

*Halden Institute for Work Studies, Working Paper 24-07. R. Okafor, L. Brandt and M. Seo.*

## Summary

Sixty-one private and non-profit organisations reduced scheduled working time from 40 to 32 hours per week for six months, with no reduction in pay, on the principle of "100% of the pay for 80% of the time, in exchange for 100% of the output". Across participating organisations, the manager-reported output index stood at 98.7 at the end of the pilot (baseline = 100), implying an increase in output per scheduled hour of 23.4%. Revenue in the pilot period was 1.4% higher than in the same six months of the previous year. Sick days fell by 36% and resignations by 56%. Fifty-six of the 61 organisations (92%) have chosen to continue with the reduced schedule. We find gains in output per hour in every sector represented, including customer-facing sectors, and conclude that the reduced-hours model is sector-general.

## Background

Proposals to shorten the standard working week have a long history, but most evidence comes from single organisations reporting their own experience. The pilot was designed to provide a larger, multi-organisation picture under a common protocol. Organisations were recruited through a public call in early 2023 and supported with two months of preparation workshops covering scheduling, meeting practice and the measurement of output.

## Design

**Participants.** Seventy organisations enrolled. Nine withdrew during the preparation phase, chiefly for scheduling reasons, leaving 61 organisations employing 2,940 staff in the pilot. Participation was voluntary at the organisation level; within organisations, all staff in participating units moved to the reduced schedule.

**Intervention.** Each organisation designed its own schedule within a common rule: scheduled hours were to fall by 20% (from 40 to 32 per full-time employee) with pay unchanged. Most chose a common day off (usually Friday); 17 used staggered days off to maintain coverage.

**Outcomes.** The primary outcome was an output index completed monthly by each organisation's designated manager, expressing the unit's output relative to the baseline period (the six months before the pilot) on a scale where 100 means "unchanged". Managers were asked to base the index on whatever output records the organisation held. Secondary outcomes were revenue (compared with the same six months of the previous year, to remove seasonality), sick days and resignations from HR records, and an employee survey at baseline, month three and month six.

**Analysis.** We report employee-weighted means. Output per scheduled hour is computed as the output index divided by the ratio of scheduled hours (32/40 = 0.8). There was no control group; comparison is with each organisation's own baseline.

## Results

### Output

Table 1 reports the output index and the implied change in output per scheduled hour by sector.

**Table 1. Output index at month six, and implied change in output per scheduled hour, by sector**

| Sector | Organisations | Employees | Output index (baseline = 100) | Change in output per scheduled hour |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Professional services | 19 | 820 | 99.8 | +24.8% |
| Software and IT | 14 | 760 | 101.2 | +26.5% |
| Marketing and media | 9 | 410 | 97.9 | +22.4% |
| Non-profit | 8 | 380 | 98.4 | +23.0% |
| Healthcare administration | 5 | 270 | 96.5 | +20.6% |
| Retail and hospitality | 6 | 300 | 93.1 | +16.4% |
| **All** | **61** | **2,940** | **98.7** | **+23.4%** |

Output was close to baseline in all sectors. Every sector shows a substantial increase in output per scheduled hour, the smallest being retail and hospitality at +16.4%.

### Revenue

Revenue, reported by 52 of the 61 organisations, was 1.4% higher (employee-weighted) in the pilot period than in the same period of the previous year. Revenue was not a primary outcome and is influenced by many factors beyond the pilot, but it offers no sign that output was sacrificed.

### Wellbeing and retention

**Table 2. Secondary outcomes**

| Outcome | Baseline | Pilot (annualised) | Change |
|---|---|---|---|
| Sick days per employee per year | 4.4 | 2.8 | −36% |
| Resignations per 100 employees per year | 7.1 | 3.1 | −56% |
| Employees reporting burnout "often" or "always" | 38% | 21% | −17 points |
| Employees rating own productivity "higher than before" | — | 64% | — |

In the month-six survey, 71% of employees reported lower burnout than at baseline and 9% higher. Self-reported energy at work, on a standardised scale, rose by 0.61 standard deviations at month three and stood 0.29 standard deviations above baseline at month six.

### Continuation

Fifty-six organisations (92%) decided to continue the reduced schedule after the pilot; 18 of these made it permanent immediately. Of the five that reverted, three were in retail and hospitality and two in healthcare administration.

## What organisations changed

Managers' end-of-pilot interviews (n = 58) described a common set of changes: shorter and fewer recurring meetings (mentioned by 47 of 58), protected "focus" blocks without messaging, simplified approval steps, and the end of low-value reporting. Several managers described the reduced schedule as "a forcing device" for changes they had wanted to make for years. We did not attempt to quantify the contribution of each change.

## Discussion

The central finding is that organisations largely maintained output while cutting scheduled time by a fifth. The implied gain in output per hour, at 23.4%, is large, and it was observed in all six sectors. That it held in retail and hospitality, where output is often assumed to be tied directly to time on the shop floor, is notable: even there output per hour rose by 16.4%. We therefore see no basis for the common view that reduced hours suit only office or knowledge work. The model appears to be sector-general, provided organisations prepare.

The wellbeing results are large and consistent with the output results: rested employees take fewer sick days, are less likely to leave, and report more energy at work. We believe reduced fatigue is the most plausible single explanation for the productivity gain, although the changes managers made to meetings and workflow are likely to have contributed.

The high continuation rate is itself evidence. Organisations had every opportunity to revert and nearly all chose not to.

## Limitations

The pilot has limitations that readers should weigh.

1. **Self-selection.** Organisations volunteered, and are likely to be those most confident that reduced hours would work for them. Results may not generalise to organisations that did not volunteer.
2. **No control group.** Comparison is with each organisation's own baseline. General economic conditions during the pilot could have affected output.
3. **Output measure.** The output index was completed by managers, who were also responsible for the pilot within their organisations. Organisations differed in what records they used.
4. **Hours.** We report scheduled hours. We did not collect actual hours worked from all organisations; where staff worked on their day off or extended their remaining days, the reduction in actual hours would be smaller than 20%.
5. **Duration.** Six months may not capture longer-run effects in either direction.

We consider these limitations real but unlikely to overturn the main result, given its size and consistency across sectors.

## Conclusion

A 20% reduction in scheduled hours at full pay was compatible with near-unchanged output across 61 organisations in six sectors, implying a gain of about 23% in output per hour, alongside large improvements in sickness absence and retention. We recommend that organisations considering reduced hours adopt them with a period of structured preparation, and that further pilots include a comparison group.

response:
I checked the numbers, and the arithmetic holds up. Every per-hour figure equals the output index divided by 0.8. The employee-weighted mean of the sector rows comes to 98.73. The organisation and employee counts sum correctly, and the percentage changes in Table 2 are right.

The problems are in what the paper concludes from those numbers. The most serious one is that the headline claim of "sector-general" is contradicted by the paper's own data.

## 1. The "sector-general" conclusion is contradicted by the data

- **Output per hour rising in every sector is almost guaranteed.** Scheduled hours fell 20%, so output per scheduled hour rises whenever output stays above 80. For a sector to show a fall, output would have to drop by more than a fifth. "Gains in every sector" therefore tells us almost nothing. The informative comparison is output against 100.
- **Retail and hospitality output fell 6.9%** (index 93.1). Pay was unchanged, so labour cost per unit of output rose by about 7.4% (1/0.931). That is the figure a retail employer cares about, and the paper never reports it. Across all organisations the equivalent rise is about 1.3%.
- **Reversion is concentrated in exactly these sectors.**
  - Retail and hospitality: 3 of 6 organisations reverted (50%).
  - Healthcare administration: 2 of 5 reverted (40%).
  - Every other sector: 0 of 50 reverted.

  This is the clearest evidence in the paper that customer-facing work is different, and the Discussion argues the opposite.
- **The sample is too small to support a general claim.** Six retail and hospitality organisations (300 staff) cannot establish that the model is "sector-general". Sectors such as manufacturing, frontline healthcare, education, logistics and the public sector are absent entirely. Even "customer-facing sectors" (plural, in the Summary) rests on one sector.

I'd remove "sector-general" from the Summary, Discussion and Conclusion. The defensible finding is roughly this: in knowledge-work sectors, managers reported output close to baseline; in retail and hospitality, output fell and half of the organisations reverted.

## 2. The 23.4% figure is an upper bound, and maybe a loose one

Limitation 4 undermines the headline more than the paper admits. The 23.4% is computed with scheduled hours, so it assumes actual hours fell by exactly 20%. If staff worked part of their day off or lengthened their other days, the true gain is smaller:

| Actual reduction in hours | Implied gain in output per hour |
|---|---|
| 20% (as assumed) | +23.4% |
| 15% | +16.1% |
| 10% | +9.7% |

You say you have actual hours from some organisations. Report them, and present the per-hour figure as a range or with a sensitivity table. Otherwise, lead with the output index rather than the per-hour number.

## 3. The primary outcome is weak, and this sits underneath everything else

- **Who did the rating:** The output index is a monthly manager rating. The managers were also responsible for the pilot, knew the intervention, and based the rating on whatever records each organisation happened to hold. This is the single biggest threat to validity.
- **Consistency doesn't remove the bias:** The Limitations section says results are "unlikely to overturn" because of their "size and consistency across sectors". But if the bias is shared (enthusiastic managers rating their own pilot), it would appear consistently across sectors too. Consistency does not reassure against a common bias.
- **"Full output" wasn't met:** At 98.7, output fell slightly. The pilot's own principle was "100% of the output", so a sentence acknowledging the shortfall would be more credible than calling it "close to baseline".
- **What the paper doesn't report:**
  - Why month six was used rather than the six-month average or the trajectory.
  - The distribution across organisations: median, range, and how many fell below 90.
  - Why organisation-level manager ratings are weighted by employee count. An organisation-weighted figure should be shown alongside.

## 4. Seasonality is handled for revenue but not for the main outcomes

Revenue is compared with the same months of the previous year "to remove seasonality". Output, sick days and resignations, however, are compared with the six months immediately before the pilot.

Recruitment ran in early 2023, followed by two months of preparation. That plausibly puts the baseline over winter and the pilot over spring to autumn. Sick days fall in summer regardless, so the 36% drop could be partly or largely seasonal. Output can also be seasonal, especially in retail and hospitality. Either use year-on-year comparisons for these outcomes as well, or explain why that isn't possible.

## 5. The revenue figure is weaker than presented

- **It is probably nominal.** In 2023, inflation in most European economies ran well above 1.4%, so revenue likely fell in real terms. "Offers no sign that output was sacrificed" doesn't follow.
- **Coverage is incomplete.** Only 52 of 61 organisations reported revenue. The paper should say which nine are missing; eight are non-profits, where "revenue" needs defining anyway. It should also say whether the missing organisations differ from the rest.

## 6. The fatigue explanation is unsupported, and partly contradicted

- **Energy is fading:** Self-reported energy rose 0.61 SD at month three but only 0.29 SD at month six, so more than half the gain disappeared within the pilot. This looks like a novelty or Hawthorne effect, and it fits poorly with "reduced fatigue is the most plausible single explanation". The Discussion should address it.
- **The process changes are a rival explanation:** Managers describe shorter meetings, focus blocks, simpler approvals and the end of low-value reporting. They call the pilot "a forcing device" for changes they had wanted for years. That suggests part of the gain might be achievable without cutting hours at all. The design cannot separate these effects, and the preparation workshops are part of the intervention. Say plainly that the mechanism is unidentified.
- **Survey details are missing:** Response rates for the baseline, month-three and month-six surveys are not reported. The 64% saying their productivity is "higher than before" has no baseline and is self-assessed by people who benefit from the policy, so it adds little.

## 7. Continuation is not independent evidence

The people deciding whether to continue are the same people who volunteered and who rated output. Reverting also has its own costs: withdrawing a valued benefit risks morale and resignations. A 92% continuation rate is therefore partly expected regardless of productivity.

Two further points:
- Only 18 of the 56 made the change permanent. The other 38 "continued", which may just mean an extended trial.
- The continuation rate is uneven by sector (see §1).

## 8. Selection and attrition

- **Withdrawals:** Nine of the 70 enrolled organisations (13%) withdrew before the pilot began. Describe them; "scheduling reasons" may itself signal sectors where the model is harder to apply.
- **Missing interviews:** Interviews cover 58 of 61 organisations. Which three are missing, and are they among the five that reverted?
- **Limitation 1 is stated but not acted on:** The Summary and Conclusion still generalise freely.

## 9. Smaller points

- **Annualising six months:** Resignation and sick-day rates are annualised from six months of data. Also note that 2023 was a cooling labour market, and that staff are unlikely to quit mid-trial while holding an unusual benefit.
- **Hours for part-time staff:** "32 per full-time employee" leaves part-time staff unexplained. Were their hours cut 20% too?
- **Who used staggered days off:** Seventeen organisations used them to maintain coverage. Report which sectors these were and whether outcomes differed.
- **Limitation 2 understates the problem:** It mentions only general economic conditions. Without a control group, seasonality, regression to the mean (organisations may have joined during a bad patch), and inflation are all uncontrolled.

## Suggested reframing of the Summary

> Sixty-one volunteer organisations cut scheduled hours by 20% at full pay for six months. Managers reported output at 98.7% of the pre-pilot level, implying up to a 23% gain in output per scheduled hour; the gain in output per hour actually worked is likely smaller because actual hours were not measured. Results were strongest in knowledge-work sectors. In retail and hospitality output fell by 7% and half the organisations reverted. Sick days and resignations fell substantially, though seasonal effects cannot be excluded. Without a control group or independent output measures, these results indicate feasibility for volunteer knowledge-work organisations rather than a general effect.

I can draft revised Discussion and Limitations sections, or add a unit-labour-cost column and a sensitivity table for actual hours to Table 1.
